title: AI Presentations
readingMarkdown:
# AI Presentations

An AI presentation tool can turn a sentence into twenty designed slides in under a minute. The slides will have a consistent theme, tidy layouts, stock photographs, and bullet points on every page. They will look professional. They will also, very often, say nothing that the audience will remember, contain a statistic nobody can trace, and look like every other AI-generated deck in the room.

The problem is not the tools. It is that a presentation is an argument, and the tools are very good at the parts of a deck that are not the argument: layout, imagery, and filler text. This chapter is about using them for those parts while keeping the argument yours. It covers the tools, the order of work that produces a deck worth sitting through, and the edits that turn a generated draft into something clear.

## 1. First-Principles Mental Model & Intuition

### A talk, with pictures

A presentation is a person making a case to an audience, with slides to help. The slides are not the presentation. A good test is whether the talk would still make sense with the projector off. If it would not, the slides have taken over a job that belongs to the speaker.

That gives the slides two jobs only. To say, at each moment, the one point being made, so that nobody is lost. And to show the evidence for it, which is often easier to see than to hear: a chart, a photograph, a diagram, a number.

### The order of work

```text
   1. THE POINT          one sentence: what should the audience believe or do?
   2. THE STORYLINE      the headlines, in order, read alone, make the case
   3. THE EVIDENCE       for each headline, the one thing that proves it
   4. THE SLIDES         layout, design, images          <- AI tools are strongest here
   5. THE CHECK          every number traced, every slide readable, the timing tested
```

Most AI-generated decks are made in the opposite order. The tool is given a topic, step 4 happens first, and steps 1 to 3 never happen at all. The result is a deck of tidy slides with topic labels for titles, "Market Analysis", "Our Solution", "Next Steps", and paragraphs of plausible bullet points beneath.

Doing steps 1 to 3 yourself, and then giving the tool your storyline, reverses that. The tool then does what it is good at, and the deck says what you mean.

### Two kinds of slide title

| A topic label | An assertion |
|---|---|
| "Returns" | "Returns fell by a third after we added video guides" |
| "Survey results" | "Four in ten customers would pay for sharpening" |
| "Costs" | "The service uses equipment we already own" |

A label says what a slide is about. An assertion says what the slide shows. Read a deck's assertions in order and you have the argument. Read its labels in order and you have a table of contents.

## 2. Core Theory, Mathematical Foundations & Architecture Internals

### The tools

At the time of writing (November 2026), AI presentation features come in three forms.

| Kind | Examples | Strength | Weakness |
|---|---|---|---|
| Dedicated generators | Gamma, Beautiful.ai | Fast, well-designed first drafts, easy sharing | Export to standard slide files can lose layout |
| Assistants inside slide software | Copilot in PowerPoint, Gemini in Google Slides | Work in the format your organisation already uses | Drafts tend to be plainer |
| General design tools | Canva | Strong templates and imagery | Less help with structure |

General chat models can also produce slide content as an outline, or write code that generates a slide file.

The landscape moves quickly. One well-funded AI presentation start-up, Tome, closed its presentation product in 2025 and turned to a different business, which is a reminder that a deck should never live only inside a tool that may disappear. Keep the outline and the evidence in your own documents, and export the finished slides.

### Answer first

Business writing has a long tradition, associated with Barbara Minto's pyramid principle, of putting the conclusion first and the support beneath it. An audience that knows where the talk is going can judge each piece of evidence as it arrives. An audience made to wait for the conclusion spends the talk guessing.

| Part | Content |
|---|---|
| **The answer** | One sentence: what you want the audience to believe or do |
| **Situation** | What everyone already agrees on |
| **Complication** | What has changed, or the problem |
| **The supports** | Three or so reasons the answer is right, each a headline |
| **The evidence** | Under each support, the fact that proves it |
| **The answer again** | The ask, now that the case has been made |

A deck built this way can be summarised from its titles alone. That makes it easy to check, easy to cut to fit a shorter slot, and easy for someone who missed the meeting to understand.

### Assertion and evidence

The assertion-evidence approach, developed and taught by Michael Alley for technical presentations, turns that structure into a slide design. Each slide has a full-sentence headline stating its claim, and beneath it visual evidence, a chart, a photograph, a diagram, in place of a list of bullet points.

The reasoning draws on research into how people learn from words and pictures together, associated particularly with Richard Mayer. Three of its principles bear on slides. People learn better when material that does not serve the point is left out, the **coherence** principle. They learn better when the important parts are signalled, the **signalling** principle, which a headline does. And they learn worse when the same words are presented as on-screen text and as speech at once, the **redundancy** principle, which is the case against reading bullet points aloud.

### Bullet walls

A slide with seven bullet points of twelve words each asks the audience to read over eighty words while also listening to a speaker. They will do one or the other, and usually they will read, ahead of the speaker, and stop listening.

AI tools produce bullet walls by default, because filling a template with text is the easiest thing for them to do. The text is typically generic: "leverage", "comprehensive", "innovative", "best-in-class". Section 3 builds a detector. Working limits are a judgement, and a common one is no more than about five bullets and forty words a slide, with fewer for a talk and more only for a deck meant to be read without a speaker.

A deck meant to be read alone, sent ahead of a meeting, is a different document. Some organisations ban slides for decisions altogether and write a narrative memo instead, on the grounds that full sentences force reasoning that bullet points hide. If the deck will be read and not presented, consider whether it should be a document.

### Numbers that came from nowhere

AI tools fill slides with statistics. Asked for a slide on customer satisfaction, a model will supply a percentage, and the percentage will look exactly like a real one. Module 1.10 explained why: fluent, confident output is no signal of accuracy.

The defence is mechanical. Every number in the deck should appear in a source you can name. A simple comparison, the numbers in the deck against the numbers in the source documents, finds the ones that came from nowhere. It cannot prove that a traced number is used correctly. It reliably catches the most embarrassing kind of error, the invented one.

### Pace

A common rule of thumb is about one to two minutes per slide for a spoken presentation. Fewer seconds than that and slides flash past. Far more and the audience stares at one slide while the speaker moves on.

For a talk of $M$ minutes with $n$ slides, each slide is on screen for an average of

$$
\frac{60\,M}{n} \text{ seconds}
$$

A generated deck of forty slides for a ten-minute slot gives fifteen seconds a slide, which is a slideshow, not a talk. The fix is almost always fewer slides, which the answer-first structure makes easy: keep the supports and their evidence, and cut everything else.

### Design and accessibility

The contrast rule from Module 6.7 applies: text at least 4.5 times the luminance contrast of its background, and 3 for large text. Projected slides lose contrast in a lit room, so aim well above the minimum. Text must be large enough to read from the back of the room: a common working floor is about 24 points for body text in a projected talk. Every image that carries meaning needs alt text, which most slide tools support, for anyone reading the deck with a screen reader.

### What AI is good for here

| Task | AI | You |
|---|---|---|
| Finding the point | Can ask questions that sharpen it | Decide it |
| Storyline | Can propose headlines from your notes | Choose and order them |
| Evidence | Can find and summarise sources | Check every number |
| Layout and design | Excellent: layouts, themes, consistent styling | Choose a template, override when needed |
| Charts | Can draw a chart from your data | Check that it shows what the headline claims |
| Speaker notes | Can draft them from the slides | Rewrite in your own words, and rehearse |
| Variants | A shorter version, a version for another audience | Decide what to cut |

### Complexity

Each check in the lab is linear in the number of slides or the length of the text. The real cost of a presentation is the audience's time: a twenty-minute talk to ten people is over three hours of attention, which is the best argument for making it shorter and clearer.

## 3. Production-Grade Implementation & Annotated Walkthrough

First, headlines.

```python
import re

GENERIC = {"introduction", "overview", "agenda", "background", "results", "conclusion", "conclusions", "summary",
           "key takeaways", "next steps", "thank you", "questions", "q&a", "market analysis", "our solution"}

def lint_headline(headline):
    words, problems = headline.split(), []
    if headline.strip().lower().rstrip(".!?:") in GENERIC:
        problems.append("generic-label")
    elif len(words) < 4:
        problems.append("too-short")
    if len(words) > 15:
        problems.append("too-long")
    return problems

for headline in ("Market analysis", "Sales", "Returns fell by a third after we added video guides",
                 "Our new sharpening service would pay for itself in eight months if half of last year's chisel buyers used it once a year",
                 "Customers want sharp tools, not more tools"):
    print(lint_headline(headline), "|", headline[:45])
```

- **A headline fails if it is a generic label.** "Market analysis", "Next steps", and their kind say what a slide is about, never what it shows. AI tools use them by default.
- **A headline under four words is too short to be an assertion.** "Sales" is a topic. A claim about sales needs a subject and a verb at the least.
- **A headline over fifteen words is too long to read at a glance.** The sharpening service sentence is a fine claim and belongs in the speaker's mouth or split across two slides.
- **The two good headlines pass.** "Returns fell by a third after we added video guides" and "Customers want sharp tools, not more tools" are each a claim that the slide below should prove.
- **The check is about form.** It cannot tell whether a claim is true or whether the slide's evidence supports it. Reading the headlines aloud in order, and asking whether they make the case, is the real test.

Next, bullet walls and untraced numbers.

```python
NUMBER = re.compile(r"\d[\d,]*(?:\.\d+)?")

def bullet_load(slides, max_words=40, max_bullets=5):
    report = []
    for number, slide in enumerate(slides, start=1):
        bullets = slide.get("bullets", [])
        words = sum(len(bullet.split()) for bullet in bullets)
        problems = []
        if len(bullets) > max_bullets:
            problems.append(f"bullets:{len(bullets)}")
        if words > max_words:
            problems.append(f"words:{words}")
        if problems:
            report.append((number, problems))
    return report

def untraced_numbers(deck_text, sources):
    def numbers(text):
        return {found.replace(",", "") for found in NUMBER.findall(text)}
    known = set().union(*(numbers(source) for source in sources)) if sources else set()
    return sorted(numbers(deck_text) - known, key=lambda value: (float(value), value))

SLIDES = [
    {"headline": "Returns fell by a third after we added video guides",
     "bullets": ["Returns fell from 9 percent to 6 percent", "Video guides were added in March"]},
    {"headline": "Our approach",
     "bullets": ["Our innovative and comprehensive approach leverages cutting-edge technology to deliver unparalleled value",
                 "We are committed to excellence across every touchpoint of the customer journey",
                 "Synergies between teams enable scalable growth", "Customer satisfaction remains our north star",
                 "We empower stakeholders", "Best-in-class outcomes", "Going forward we will continue to iterate"]},
]
SOURCE = "In 2025 we sold 1,240 chisels. 112 were returned, a rate of 9 percent. After the video guides in March 2026, returns fell to 6 percent."
DECK = "Returns fell from 9% to 6% after the video guides. We sold 1,240 chisels in 2025. Customer satisfaction rose 23%. The market is worth 4.5 billion."
print(bullet_load(SLIDES))
print(untraced_numbers(DECK, [SOURCE]))
```

- **`bullet_load` counts bullets and words on every slide.** It reports the slides over either limit, numbered from 1.
- **The first slide passes.** Two short bullets that support its headline.
- **The second slide fails both limits.** Seven bullets and 48 words, nearly all of them filler, under a headline that is a label. This is a typical generated slide, and nothing on it could be shown to be true or false.
- **`untraced_numbers` collects every number in the deck and in the sources.** Commas are removed so that "1,240" matches "1240". It returns the numbers that appear in the deck and in no source.
- **Two numbers are untraced.** "23" percent and "4.5" billion appear nowhere in the shop's figures. Either someone has a source for them, which should then be added, or the tool invented them.
- **The check is literal.** It would flag "7.0" if the source said "7", and it would miss a real number used wrongly. It catches the invented statistic, which is the error that does the most damage when someone in the audience asks where it came from.

Then, a deck in answer-first order.

```python
def pyramid(answer, supports):
    slides = [{"role": "title", "headline": answer, "bullets": []},
              {"role": "agenda", "headline": f"The case in {len(supports)} points", "bullets": [headline for headline, _ in supports]}]
    slides += [{"role": "support", "headline": headline, "bullets": list(evidence)} for headline, evidence in supports]
    slides.append({"role": "close", "headline": answer, "bullets": []})
    return slides

SUPPORTS = [
    ("Most returns come from blunt edges, not faults", ["68 of 112 returns cited a blunt edge"]),
    ("Customers will pay for sharpening", ["41 percent of a 300-customer survey said yes at 8 pounds"]),
    ("The service uses kit we already own", ["Two stones and a strop, already in the workshop"]),
]
DECK_PLAN = pyramid("A sharpening service would cut returns and pay for itself", SUPPORTS)
for slide in DECK_PLAN:
    print(slide["role"], "|", slide["headline"])
```

- **The first slide is the answer.** The partners know from the start what they are being asked to agree to.
- **The second lists the supports.** It is the whole argument on one slide: a reader who sees nothing else knows the case.
- **Each support gets a slide with its evidence.** One claim, one proof.
- **The last slide repeats the answer.** After the evidence, the ask is the natural ending.
- **Six slides.** That is the right size for a ten-minute decision. A generated deck on the same subject would likely run to fifteen or twenty, most of them labels.
- **The structure is what to give an AI tool.** Pasting these six headlines and their evidence into a presentation generator, and asking it to design the slides, puts the tool to work on layout while the argument stays yours.

Finally, pace.

```python
def pace(slide_count, minutes, low=30, high=180):
    if slide_count <= 0:
        raise ValueError("a deck needs at least one slide")
    seconds = round(minutes * 60 / slide_count, 1)
    verdict = "rushed" if seconds < low else "slow" if seconds > high else "ok"
    return {"seconds_per_slide": seconds, "verdict": verdict}

print(pace(40, 10), pace(6, 10), pace(3, 20))
```

- **The average time per slide is the talk's length divided by the number of slides.**
- **Forty slides in ten minutes is fifteen seconds each, which is rushed.** That is what many generated decks look like when presented.
- **Six slides in ten minutes is 100 seconds each.** Comfortably within the range.
- **Three slides in twenty minutes is 400 seconds each, which is slow.** The audience looks at one slide for nearly seven minutes.
- **The limits of 30 and 180 seconds are deliberately wide, and the target is still one to two minutes.** A fast-paced talk with many image slides can run quicker. A workshop that discusses each slide can run slower. The figure is a prompt to look.

**Complexity.** Every function is linear in the slides or the text.

### A brief for an AI presentation tool

```text
AUDIENCE:   [who, what they know, what they will decide]
TIME:       [minutes]  ->  [n] slides at 1 to 2 minutes each
ANSWER:     [one sentence]
STORYLINE:  use exactly these headlines, in this order:
            1. [answer]
            2. [the case in N points]
            3. [support 1]  evidence: [fact, with its source]
            4. [support 2]  evidence: [fact, with its source]
            5. [support 3]  evidence: [fact, with its source]
            6. [answer, as the ask]
RULES:      headlines as written. At most 3 short bullets per slide, or a chart.
            Do not add statistics. Use no stock photos of people in suits.
DESIGN:     [template or brand colours], body text at least 24 pt, contrast at least 4.5
```

### Before presenting

| Check | Pass |
|---|---|
| Read the headlines alone, in order | They make the case |
| Every headline | An assertion, not a label |
| Every slide | At most about five bullets and forty words, or a visual instead |
| Every number | Appears in a named source |
| Every chart | Shows what its headline claims |
| Pace | One to two minutes a slide |
| Projector off | The talk still makes sense |
| From the back of the room | The text is readable |

## 4. Practitioner Wisdom & Edge Cases (Reddit / HN / Stack Overflow Synthesis)

**Starting in the tool.** Typing a topic into a generator gives a deck about the topic, not a case for anything. Write the answer and the headlines first.

**Accepting the first draft.** A generated deck is a starting point with the structure of a template. Expect to delete half the slides and rewrite every headline.

**Bullet walls.** Seven bullets of corporate filler on a slide guarantee that nobody listens to the speaker. Cut to the claim and its proof, or replace the bullets with a chart.

**Reading the slides aloud.** If the speaker says what the slide already says, the audience reads ahead and stops listening. The slide shows the evidence. The speaker explains it.

**Invented statistics.** The most common and most damaging error in AI decks. A plausible percentage that nobody can source destroys trust in everything else on the slide. Trace every number.

**Generic stock imagery.** Handshakes, lightbulbs, and people pointing at screens tell the audience the deck was assembled, not thought about. Use a real photograph, a chart of your data, or nothing.

**Too many slides.** Generators produce long decks because slides are cheap to make. They are not cheap to sit through. Cut to what the time allows.

**Labels for titles.** "Results", "Analysis", "Next steps" waste the most-read line on each slide. Write what the slide shows.

**Charts that do not support the headline.** A generated chart can look right and show something else. Check that the chart, read alone, makes the headline's point.

**Text too small for the room.** A slide that is readable on a laptop is not readable on a projector at the back of a hall. Check at the distance of the furthest seat.

**Losing the deck with the tool.** Presentations kept only inside a hosted generator vanish with it, and export to standard formats can scramble layouts. Keep the outline in a document and export the finished deck.

**A deck that should be a document.** If the slides will be read without a speaker, they need full sentences, and at that point they are a memo with page breaks. Write the memo.

## 5. Active Recall Check & Synthesis Summary

**Summary.** A presentation is an argument with slides to help, and the slides have two jobs: to state the point being made and to show its evidence. AI tools are excellent at layout, design, and consistent styling and, left to themselves, produce decks of topic labels, bullet walls, generic imagery, and invented numbers, because they start from a topic and not from a case. Reversing the order fixes this: decide the one-sentence answer, write the storyline as full-sentence headlines in answer-first order, attach one piece of evidence to each, and only then give that structure to the tool. Assertion headlines, visual evidence in place of bullets, and speaking to the slides instead of reading them follow from research on how people learn from words and pictures. Every number in a deck should be traced to a named source, and a simple comparison of numbers catches the invented ones. Pace is the talk's length over its slide count, about one to two minutes a slide, and generated decks are usually far too long. Contrast, type size, and alt text keep slides readable for everyone.

**Question 1.** An AI tool produced a 32-slide deck for a 12-minute slot. Its slide titles include "Overview", "Market Analysis", "Our Solution", "Benefits", "Next Steps", and "Thank You". Compute the pace, explain what the titles tell you, and describe how you would rebuild the deck.

<details>
<summary>View Answer</summary>

Twelve minutes is 720 seconds, and over 32 slides that is 22.5 seconds a slide, which is well under the half-minute floor and far from the one to two minutes a spoken presentation usually needs. The deck would feel like slides flashing past while the speaker hurried to keep up. The titles are generic labels: each says what a slide is about and none says what it shows. Read in order, they are a table of contents for any presentation on any subject, which means the tool built the deck from a template and a topic, with no argument behind it. The slides beneath such titles are usually bullet walls of plausible filler. To rebuild it, start away from the tool. Write the one-sentence answer: what the audience should believe or do at the end. Write three supports, each a full-sentence assertion that would convince this audience, and attach to each the single strongest piece of evidence, with its source. That gives a deck of about six slides: the answer, the case in three points, three support slides, and the ask. At twelve minutes, that is about ninety seconds a slide with three minutes left for questions. Then give those headlines and the evidence to the tool, with instructions to use the headlines exactly, to add no statistics, and to use a chart or photograph where possible instead of bullets. Finally, check every number against its source, read the headlines aloud in order to confirm they make the case, and rehearse with the projector off.

</details>

**Question 2.** A generated slide reads: "Customer satisfaction has increased 37% year over year, driven by our customer-centric approach and industry-leading service." The company's own figures show a satisfaction score of 7.8 out of 10 last year and 8.1 this year. What is wrong, and what should the slide say?

<details>
<summary>View Answer</summary>

The 37 percent does not come from the company's figures. A score rising from 7.8 to 8.1 is an increase of 0.3 points, which is about 3.8 percent of the starting value. The tool produced a number that looked like a real statistic and attached it to the subject, and a check of the deck's numbers against the source data would flag it as untraced. If presented, it would be wrong by a factor of ten, and anyone who knew the real figures would distrust the rest of the deck. The rest of the sentence is also empty. "Customer-centric approach" and "industry-leading service" are claims with no evidence, the generic language AI tools fill slides with, and "driven by" asserts a cause that nothing shows. A corrected slide states what the data supports, as an assertion headline: "Customer satisfaction rose from 7.8 to 8.1 out of 10 this year." If the company knows the reason, and has evidence for it, the evidence goes on the slide: for example, "The rise followed the March launch of video guides, and complaints about blunt tools fell by half over the same period", with the source named. If it does not know the reason, the slide should not claim one. A small chart of the two scores, or of the score by quarter, would show the change more clearly than any sentence.

</details>

**Question 3.** A manager asks you to turn a ten-page proposal into a deck "with AI, quickly" for a 15-minute board meeting. Describe how you would divide the work between yourself and the tool, and what you would check before presenting.

<details>
<summary>View Answer</summary>

The part I would keep is deciding the case. I would read the proposal and write its answer in one sentence, what the board should approve. Then I would choose the three or four reasons that would most persuade this board, each as a full-sentence headline, and for each pick the single strongest piece of evidence from the proposal, noting the page it came from. A model can help here as an assistant: asked to list the proposal's main claims and the numbers that support them, it gives a useful checklist, but the choice of what this audience needs to hear is mine. Fifteen minutes allows about seven to ten slides at one and a half to two minutes each, so the structure is the answer, the case in a few points, a slide per support, perhaps a slide on cost or risk if the board will ask, and the ask. The part I would give the tool is building the slides from that structure: layout, a consistent design in the company's template, charts from the proposal's tables, and draft speaker notes. My instructions would say to use the headlines exactly, to add no statistics or claims, to use charts and not bullet lists where possible, and to keep body text large. Before presenting I would check that every number on every slide appears in the proposal, that every chart shows what its headline says, that the headlines read alone make the case, that no slide has more than a few short bullets, and that the text is readable at the size it will be projected. I would rewrite the speaker notes in my own words, rehearse once against the clock, and send the board the proposal itself as the document to read, since the deck is for the meeting and the detail belongs in the paper.

</details>

interactiveLab.context: A shop owner has to present a case for a new sharpening service to two partners and has an AI tool that will produce a deck in seconds. assert _deck[0] == {"role": "title", "headline": _answer, "bullets": []} and _deck[-1] == {"role": "close", "headline": _answer, "bullets": []}, "The answer opens and closes the deck"

_evidence.append("added later")

steps.instruction: Implement pace(slide_count, minutes, low, high). If the slide count is zero or less, raise ValueError. The seconds per slide are the minutes times 60 divided by the slide count, rounded to 1 decimal place. The verdict is 'rushed' if that is below low, 'slow' if it is above high, and 'ok' otherwise. Return a dict with 'seconds_per_slide' and 'verdict'. Compare 40 slides in 10 minutes, 6 slides in 10 minutes, and 3 slides in 20 minutes. This is the pace formula from Section 2. [MOD-6.11]

"""
Lab solution: Headlines, Bullet Load, Untraced Numbers, a Pyramid, and Pace
Standard library only.
"""
import re

GENERIC = {"introduction", "overview", "agenda", "background", "results", "conclusion", "conclusions", "summary",
           "key takeaways", "next steps", "thank you", "questions", "q&a", "market analysis", "our solution"}

NUMBER = re.compile(r"\d[\d,]*(?:\.\d+)?")

SLIDES = [
    {"headline": "Returns fell by a third after we added video guides",
     "bullets": ["Returns fell from 9 percent to 6 percent", "Video guides were added in March"]},
    {"headline": "Our approach",
     "bullets": ["Our innovative and comprehensive approach leverages cutting-edge technology to deliver unparalleled value",
                 "We are committed to excellence across every touchpoint of the customer journey",
                 "Synergies between teams enable scalable growth", "Customer satisfaction remains our north star",
                 "We empower stakeholders", "Best-in-class outcomes", "Going forward we will continue to iterate"]},
]

SOURCE = "In 2025 we sold 1,240 chisels. 112 were returned, a rate of 9 percent. After the video guides in March 2026, returns fell to 6 percent."
DECK = "Returns fell from 9% to 6% after the video guides. We sold 1,240 chisels in 2025. Customer satisfaction rose 23%. The market is worth 4.5 billion."

SUPPORTS = [
    ("Most returns come from blunt edges, not faults", ["68 of 112 returns cited a blunt edge"]),
    ("Customers will pay for sharpening", ["41 percent of a 300-customer survey said yes at 8 pounds"]),
    ("The service uses kit we already own", ["Two stones and a strop, already in the workshop"]),
]


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- Step 1
def lint_headline(headline):
    """A label says what a slide is about. An assertion says what it shows. The check is
    about form: whether the claim is true is for a person to judge."""
    words, problems = headline.split(), []
    if headline.strip().lower().rstrip(".!?:") in GENERIC:
        problems.append("generic-label")
    elif len(words) < 4:
        problems.append("too-short")
    if len(words) > 15:
        problems.append("too-long")
    return problems


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- Step 2
def bullet_load(slides, max_words=40, max_bullets=5):
    """An audience asked to read eighty words while listening will do one or the other,
    and usually it reads ahead and stops listening."""
    report = []
    for number, slide in enumerate(slides, start=1):
        bullets = slide.get("bullets", [])
        words = sum(len(bullet.split()) for bullet in bullets)
        problems = []
        if len(bullets) > max_bullets:
            problems.append(f"bullets:{len(bullets)}")
        if words > max_words:
            problems.append(f"words:{words}")
        if problems:
            report.append((number, problems))
    return report


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- Step 3
def untraced_numbers(deck_text, sources):
    """Literal and blunt: it misses a real number used wrongly, and it catches the invented
    statistic, which does the most damage when someone asks where it came from."""
    def numbers(text):
        return {found.replace(",", "") for found in NUMBER.findall(text)}
    known = set().union(*(numbers(source) for source in sources)) if sources else set()
    return sorted(numbers(deck_text) - known, key=lambda value: (float(value), value))


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- Step 4
def pyramid(answer, supports):
    """Answer first, then the case in a few points, a slide per support with its evidence,
    and the answer again as the ask. This structure is what to hand to an AI design tool."""
    slides = [{"role": "title", "headline": answer, "bullets": []},
              {"role": "agenda", "headline": f"The case in {len(supports)} points", "bullets": [headline for headline, _ in supports]}]
    slides += [{"role": "support", "headline": headline, "bullets": list(evidence)} for headline, evidence in supports]
    slides.append({"role": "close", "headline": answer, "bullets": []})
    return slides


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- Step 5
def pace(slide_count, minutes, low=30, high=180):
    """Generated decks are usually far too long for their slot. The fix is almost always
    fewer slides."""
    if slide_count <= 0:
        raise ValueError("a deck needs at least one slide")
    seconds = round(minutes * 60 / slide_count, 1)
    verdict = "rushed" if seconds < low else "slow" if seconds > high else "ok"
    return {"seconds_per_slide": seconds, "verdict": verdict}


if __name__ == "__main__":
    for headline in ("Market analysis", "Sales", "Returns fell by a third after we added video guides",
                     "Our new sharpening service would pay for itself in eight months if half of last year's chisel buyers used it once a year",
                     "Customers want sharp tools, not more tools"):
        print(lint_headline(headline), "|", headline[:45])

    print(bullet_load(SLIDES))
    print(untraced_numbers(DECK, [SOURCE]))

    plan = pyramid("A sharpening service would cut returns and pay for itself", SUPPORTS)
    for slide in plan:
        print(slide["role"], "|", slide["headline"])

    print(pace(40, 10), pace(6, 10), pace(3, 20))
    print(pace(32, 12), round((8.1 - 7.8) / 7.8 * 100, 1), round(1 - 6 / 9, 3))
